The opening slide identifies the training as FORTNA OptiSweep Training - Day 2. The segment is timestamped from 00:00:00.000 to 00:00:03.000 and includes the date 2026-03-18.
The slide contains the note: "Morning Location is Different." No specific locations or additional scheduling details are provided in the source segment.
The opening slide shows the date and time as 2026-03-18 13:26 UTC. It lists Mitchel Flynn under "Recorded by" and Samuel Prescott under "Organized by."

The presenter states that the training will cover message flow, the database, API, Ignition, and services. The segment does not provide detailed architecture, configuration, operational behavior, or access information for these areas.

The slide contents list Message Flow, Database, and API as numbered training sections. No message types, database entities, interfaces, endpoints, data structures, or operating instructions are provided in this segment.

The slide contents list Ignition as section 7 and Service as section 8. The transcript also refers to Ignition and services as subjects for review. This segment does not describe screens, service names, service states, dependencies, configuration, or operating procedures.

The architecture includes an XLe chat communication module, Sorter Sweeper module, Robotics module, Geek+ comm module, XLe chat OBC communication, sorter and tipper PLCs, Ignition OPC server, Aveva HMI, SQL Server, scanners, ASX, and printers. The training describes the OptiSweep software as Windows services running on a server.

The training describes XLe chat as the mechanism used for secure communication through an S tunnel. Within OptiSweep, the XLe chat module communicates with the XLe chat OBC communication module. The OBC communication module subscribes to Ignition tags, enabling OptiSweep to read and write tipper-related data.

The module tracks packages as they come in, updates associated information, and tracks the tote at the tipper. It makes requests to the Robotics module for actions such as picking up a tote, moving a tote out, and dropping off a tote.

The Sorter Sweeper module sends requests such as pick up tote, move out tote, and drop off tote to the Robotics module. The Robotics module runs these requests through configured maps, including sorter and tipper queue and execution areas. The Geek+ comm module is intended to support vendor flexibility by translating Robotics module commands into the format required by Geek+ and sending them as HTTP/REST API requests.

The training identifies Ignition as the HMI base and references an Ignition OPC server in the architecture. Ignition collects data and sends it to Aveva for UPS. The architecture also shows TCP connections involving the OPC server, PLCs, and Aveva HMI.

Sorter Sweeper receives data from sorter tippers, hospital stations, and the HMI; creates tote tasks for the Sorter Robotics module; processes data from the hospital; and notifies tippers about tote arrivals or robot faults. The transcript identifies tote tasks including induct tote, remove tote, pick up tote, move out sorter, drop off sorter, and drop off hospital.

Sorter Robotics receives tote tasks from Sorter Sweeper and generates commands for Geek Plus. The transcript lists AGV-related commands including initialize AGV, empty, go to, pick up tote, move tote, drop off tote, cancel request, and go charge.

The OPC COM module manages communication between the Robotics module and the Geek Plus RMS server. It also uses Ignition's built-in tag provider to connect to the hospital and tippers and relay relevant tags. The module subscribes to OPC server tags, sends tag updates to Sorter Sweeper for processing, and writes data received from Sorter Sweeper back to the OPC server.

The source describes XLE as the UPS version of WCS and identifies XLE COM as the communication layer between Sorter Sweeper and the UPS Chat server. The UPS Chat communication includes tote, destination, scan, sort, close, and printer-related messages. The source also identifies scan tunnel data, parcel dimensions, load category, possible destinations, final destination, and sort confirmation as exchanged information.

The source identifies scan tunnel data as including parcel dimensions and load category. Sort information is sent from XLE, possible destinations are collected for each parcel, and sort confirmation is sent from the sorter. The source also references hot bin close-out messages, Sure Post load notification, destination closed messages, and print-label data supplied by XLE. These are described as communication concepts rather than a complete operating procedure.
The provided source identifies a training video slide labeled "Database Walkthrough" and does not provide further operational details about the database, its screens, or its use.
The slide identifies the Robotics module as the state machine for AGVs. It receives tote tasks from the SorterSweeper module and generates commands for Geek+ to execute those tasks.

The detailed design slide lists the following AGV command concepts: induct tote, remove tote, pickup tote, move tote, drop off tote, cancel request, and go charge. The source does not define command syntax or execution procedures.

The diagram shows the Geek+ Comm Module alongside the Robotics and SorterSweeper modules. The Robotics module generates commands for Geek+ to execute tote tasks, and the diagram includes robot notifications and command results among the related message concepts.

The speaker states, “All right, we're gonna walk through all the tables.” The associated slide is labeled “Database Walkthrough.” No table names, schemas, fields, or operating procedures are provided in this segment.
The transcript refers collectively to “all the tables.” The source does not identify individual tables or describe their contents, relationships, retention, or usage.

The captured slide frame at 00:08:52.500 contains the OCR text “Database Walkthrough” and is associated with the transcript introducing a review of all tables. The frame does not provide additional technical detail.

The training describes the WCS as providing data containers, entity logs, and PLC communication. It identifies OptiSweep-related databases as Audit, Geek AGV, OPC Comms, Robotics, and Sworder Sweeper, with SQL Jobs used primarily for cleanup. The database structure is described as compartmentalized across multiple tables and databases.

The training states that OptiSweep utilizes EntityLogs for logging. The DeveloperLogs table records information such as the message, level, exception, trace ID, host and instance names, assembly and class names, method name, and line number. These fields support identifying what information was logged, where in the code it originated, and error details.

The Audit database tracks the AGDID, current Geek task ID, and command GUID sent by the robotics engine. Changes to the relevant table are tracked in an audits table. The Geek AGV database contains an action-logging model that logs tasks to Geek Plus and serves as a history of tasks.

The lattice code model stores lattice codes and their respective station IDs. When a tote is inducted or dropped off, Geek requires a lattice code for the location. The Geek COM module uses the table to convert a station ID from robotics module requests to the corresponding lattice code. Geek also requires a unit identifier for each location.

The OPC configuration table stores connection parameters required for the software to bridge to OPC. The OPC tags table stores tags that are subscribed to at startup. The training describes these records as covering the information required to connect to OPC and the tags that are written to and read from.

The model includes the station number, occupancy state, zone, closeout zone, location type, maximum number of AGVs allowed at the location, and whether dwell time should be tracked. The training describes the orange locations shown in RMS as including workstation or station identifiers.

The listed location types include sorter entrance queue, sorter queue, sorter exit queue, tipper, tipper queue, tipper exit queue, hospital drop-off, hospital entrance queue, hospital pickup, hospital exit, queue shutdown, off-the-end shutdown queue, GLD pre-queue, and GLD pre-queue exit. The transcript also refers to location statuses and occupancy as model attributes, but does not provide a complete status enumeration.

The slide identifies the model fields as Name, EntranceId, ExitId, TipperCount, and Disabled. The displayed examples are SorterSide 1a with entrance 46, exit 44, tipper count 4, disabled 0; SorterSide 1b with entrance 246, exit 244, tipper count 4, disabled 0; SorterSide 2a with entrance 446, exit 444, tipper count 4, disabled 0; and SorterSide 2b with entrance 648, exit 646, tipper count 4, disabled 1.

A sorter side is described as being associated with a group of tippers. The transcript explains that tipper count can represent the closest four tippers and that assignment uses another mapping. The stated purpose is to balance traffic and volume across sorter sides and operator stations, while also supporting more even tipper utilization for maintenance planning. The training mentions an example in which one sorter side is disabled, but does not provide a complete configuration procedure.

Zones are described as a system concept used on the sorter side, with the transcript referring to seven zones in the example shown. Cell codes are compared with RMS node codes and are described as terminology intended to remain modular across vendors. The location data also includes XY coordinates, described in the transcript as centimeter-based coordinates.

The slide is titled "Robotics Database Overview" and displays database entities associated with robots, commands, locations, charging, system errors, tasks, totes, stations, sorters, and activity records. A separate "HospitalDatabaseModel" label is also visible in the slide content. The source does not define the database schema or provide access instructions.

Visible OCR and slide content include Robot, RobotCommand, RobotCommandActivity, RobotLocation, RobotTaskActivity, and related fields such as RobotCode, RobotName or AgvName, CommandGuid, CommandId, TaskGuid, TaskName, TaskType, TaskStatus, Status, SentTime, InProgressTime, ExecutedTime, StartTime, FinishTime, and TotalTime. These are presented as database entities or fields; the source does not define their complete relationships or operational meaning.

The slide visibly lists Charging Thresholds, ChargingLocations, LocationActiveDwell, LocationDwellActivity, ChargeKick, SystemErrorDefinition, SystemErrorActivity, SystemActiveError, SystemErrorDescription, SystemErrorResolution, AgvErrorActivity, Task, TaskStatus, Tote, ToteStatus, TipperStation, Sorter, and SorterSideTipperStation. Other visible fields include Battery, Temperature, ErrorCode, Error, Cause, Critical, Disabled, Station, Area, Zone, Sequence, and TotalTime. The source presents these as database entities or fields and does not explain their procedures, thresholds, or relationships.

A sorter side may be associated with a variable number of nearby tippers. The discussion describes configurations involving two operator stations, each with left and right sides, resulting in four tipper arms, as well as earlier configurations with three operator stations and a tipper count of three. The mapping is based on proximity to the sorter exit and may be adjusted for site layout.

The training states that the initial configuration file is a CSV file used to populate the database. Sorter sides that are not included in an initial phase are disabled, and later phases can be enabled through a database update using a phase-based script. A disabled sorter side remains part of the configured model and can participate in nearby mapping when enabled.

The sort locations database model contains sorted locations and their respective queue locations. Queue locations are positioned behind sorted locations and are used by AGVs with an empty tote to fill a location when an exchange occurs. The table also records the associated sorter side and the sequence of locations from the sorter entrance queue.

The shutdown staging table maps where AGVs are staged during a shutdown state. The training describes separate staging concepts for AGVs with totes and AGVs without totes. AGVs with totes use an off-the-end queue associated with the sorter, while AGVs without totes are mapped to sorter locations or available shutdown queue locations. The table therefore represents shutdown-related staging locations and tote-status distinctions.

The training discussion describes sequence values from 1 through 4 beginning at the sorter entrance queue. A zone sequence, such as sequence 4, is used as a lookup value to identify the corresponding sorter station or location. The mapping is described as a lookup table rather than a robot command.

The discussion refers to a sorter zone exit queue sequence ID and notes that the collection may also be considered an array. The terminology is treated as interchangeable for describing the ordered set of AGVs associated with sorter zones.

The training states that AGVs in the same zone need to remain together when the queue is compressed. The software is described as handling the compression, while the sequence mapping represents the intended order and zone association.

The screen capture shows the RMS Map Monitor with a message that the system is currently in an emergency-stop state. It also includes a statement that the RMS map monitoring page triggers a system emergency stop. The visible screen contains robot information, map-monitoring controls, and an emergency-stop button label.

The charging database model includes a charging area table, a charging location table, and a charging threshold table. Together, these tables represent charging-area boundaries, individual charger mappings, tote-stand associations, and charging-related values used by the application.

The charging area database model stores charging areas and their entrance IDs and exit IDs. The training describes charging areas as having multiple chargers and includes a disabled indicator for the area.

The charging location database model stores each individual charger and the station where it is located. It also records the tote stand associated with the charger, the charging area associated with it, and whether the charger is disabled. The training describes this mapping as representing charger entrance, exit, and tote-stand placement within the layout.

The charging threshold database model stores values used in application logic to identify when an AGV needs charging, when it can leave a charger, and when emergency charging is required. The source does not specify the threshold values themselves.

The training describes sorter-side identifiers such as 1A, 1B, 2A, and 2B as model or mapping identifiers. Chargers are assigned to sorter sides; the example describes charger assignments split between two sorter sides. The source also states that an AGV normally uses chargers assigned to its sorter side, while an available charger on another sorter side may be used in an emergency situation. The training further describes cycling AGVs onto chargers to keep charger usage even and following charging requirements.

The table contains commands while they are active, including command status and timing information. The transcript describes statuses such as sent, in progress, completed, errored, and cancelled. Completed commands are archived to Robot Command Activity.

The Robotics module sends generic commands such as moving a tote to a drop-off location. The Geek Plus COM module translates these internal commands into the vendor platform's REST API format and converts responses back into the format used by OptiSweep. The transcript states that a different robot vendor could use a different translation module.

The historical record includes the command name, command status, robot name, container, station, parameters sent to the Geek Plus COM module, sent time, in-progress time, execution time, station circuit, and total time. The transcript describes the active Robot Command Database as containing current commands, while past commands can be looked up in Robot Command Activity.

The transcript describes current location ID and destination location fields in the robot database model. It also refers to maximum AGV capacity associated with robot locations or queues, including examples where a tipper may allow one or, in some cases, two AGVs. The in-progress state is discussed in relation to whether a location is considered occupied or available.

The training states that custom APIs and changes to the Geek Plus integration provide WCS with control over charging. WCS is responsible for assigning an AGV to a particular charger, while RMS does not perform that charger assignment in this configuration. A charging-related button may remain visible in the RMS user interface even though the described charging control is handled through WCS.
The source describes separate current and archived records: the Robot Task database model contains the current task information, while completed tasks are moved to Robot Task Activity.

The AGV Error model is described as a lookup or dictionary of AGV errors. It stores the error code and an associated description. Errors are classified as critical or non-critical for metric purposes. The transcript gives an example in which an error code is associated with a description such as a front bumper trigger.

Active error records include the robot code or name, error code, error description, and Sort GUID. The Sort GUID identifies the sort during which the error occurred. The source states that when an error is resolved or the AGV is removed, the record is archived to the AGVErrorActivityDatabaseModel.

A dwell record represents how long an AGV has been sitting at a tracked sort location. The Location Active Dwell model contains the current dwell, and once the AGV leaves the location, the dwell information is archived to Location Dwell Activity.

The displayed model includes AgvName, Station, and SortGuid fields. Dwell tracking is represented as a true-or-false setting for stations, and the model collects an AGV's active dwell while it remains at a tracked location.
The archived activity display includes AgvName, Station, SortGuid, Start Time, Finish Time, and Total Time. The source shows completed dwell examples with timestamps and total durations.

Hospital dwell time is described as how long an AGV waits before it can drop off its tote at the hospital. Tipper dwell time is described as how long a tote remains at the tipper before it is tipped. The discussion also references entrance queue and execution-related timing. These metrics are presented as indicators of local activity and behavior, while noting that reducing dwell at one point may affect system throughput elsewhere.

The displayed Robotics Database table includes system error names, areas, descriptions, and defined resolutions. Examples shown include AgvHasNotMoved30Seconds in the AGV area with the description "AGV has not moved in 30 seconds" and the resolution "Reboot AGV"; AgvOutOfSequence with "AGV is out of sequence"; and communication-related errors with reconnect-related resolutions.

The model presents active errors and includes information such as the error name, area, area code, and description. The displayed data includes examples from AGV and system communication areas, along with last-seen information.

The training segment explains that once an active error is resolved, it is archived to the System Error Activity model table. The displayed activity records include the system error description, system error resolution, start time, finish time, and elapsed duration.

The training material describes the SystemDatabaseModel as showing the state of the system and the current sort GUID. The displayed database query selects records from dbo.SystemDatabaseModel in the Helix2x_1Prod_Robotics database.

The training transcript lists statuses including StartingUp, StartUpRequested, Running, ShutDownRequested, Shutdown, ZoneConfigRequested, ZoneConfigStaging, CloseOutRequested, CloseOutStaging, and CloseOutStaged. The OCR display shows a current example with status Running.

The database view identifies the fields EntityInserted, EntityLastUpdate, Status, and SortGuid. The displayed record includes an insertion timestamp, a last-update timestamp, status Running, and a GUID value.

The database browser shown in the training artifact lists models including SystemDatabaseModel, RobotDatabaseModel, RobotTaskDatabaseModel, RobotCommandDatabaseModel, RobotLocationDatabaseModel, ChargingDatabaseModel, ChargingLocationsDatabaseModel, ChargingThresholdsDatabaseModel, AgvErrorModel, SystemActiveErrorModel, SystemErrorActivityModel, SortLocationsDatabaseModel, SorterSideDatabaseModel, and related activity models.

The displayed database overview includes field names such as SystemState, Destination, Active Exchange, PackageUid, Status, TrackingNumber, SorterSideName, SortGuid, Station, Zone, ToteName, RobotCode, ExchangeType, SortName, LaneName, and ErrorCode. The source does not provide a complete schema or explain relationships among these fields.

Visible field names include SorterName, SorterSideName, SorterId, LaneName, LaneStatus, Lane, Tipper, TipperStatus, TipperStation, TipperStationId, TipperLoadType, TipperDeparture, TipperSelect, and related identifiers such as SortGuid and LocationId. These terms are presented as database fields; the source does not define their exact data types or operational relationships.

The displayed fields include PackageUid, TrackingNumber, Itemid, PackageClassification, OriginalDestination, FinalDestination, Destination, ToteName, ToteId, ToteError, ToteTypeName, ToteNotFound, SortName, SortGuid, TotalSorted, StartTime, FinishTime, and TotalTime. The slide provides field names only and does not define processing behavior or validation rules.

Visible terms include SystemState, Status, TaskStatus, LaneStatus, TipperStatus, ErrorCode, ErrorCause, FaultTagPath, FaultVal, Message, Estop, Estopped, EstopActivity, EstopAreaName, Disabled, KeepChutesClosed, ReadyForExchange, and ReadyForExchangeTime. The source identifies these as database fields but does not define their meanings, thresholds, or response actions.

The database view shows multiple Helix2x_1Prod databases, including Audit, DataContainers, EntityLogs, GeekAgv, OpcComms, PlcCommunication, and Robotics. The segment transcript also states that there is not just one system.

The slide identifies dbo.SystemDatabaseModel in the Helix2x_1Prod_Robotics database. It states that the SystemDatabaseModel shows the configuration state of the system and the current sort guid. The displayed query references the SystemDatabaseModel table with a SNAPSHOT clause.

The status values visible in the database view include Running, StartingUp, StartUpRequested, ShutDownRequested, Shutdown, ZoneConfigRequested, ZoneConfigStaging, CloseOutRequested, CloseOutStaging, and CloseOutStaged. These values are shown as database status values; the source does not define their transitions or operational handling.

The sorter model includes storage-oriented data and relationships between database entities. The segment describes the model as an overview comparable to the robotics model and notes that some fields represent configuration or activities.
The XLE IP is described as the receiver IP address, and the XLE name is described as the receiver name. Both identifiers are associated with sending messages to the sorter.

Locations represent stations in the sorter map. The training segment identifies four location types: sorter, tipper, hospital, and induction. Induction and hospital locations are associated with specified tote induction and tote drop-off locations, respectively.

When an AGV reports the same cell code as an induction or hospital location, the training segment states that the hospital controller is notified of the AGV presence. The segment also describes using a station reported by the robotics engine to identify the relevant tipper and notify that tipper that a tote has arrived.

The segment describes sequence as beginning at the sorter entrance and lane as the shoot number defined by UPS. Lane status values are active, bypass, and not tracking; active is described as open and bypass as closed. Location data also includes destinations, a specified tipper indicator, and GLD-related location designation. Lane delay is described in relation to straight-line sorter diversion prediction.

The model contains a list of tags to subscribe to and act on. Tag behavior is associated with a tag type parent indicating whether the tag is an input or an output. The transcript identifies hospital, tipper, and display communications as uses of these tags.

Tags can have different data types and are commonly represented as strings in the tag model. A variable type identifies which value representation or column applies to a particular tag. This design is described as allowing additional tag types to be added through database entries rather than requiring a fixed native column for every type.

The training discussion describes the tables as settings used by the software rather than fixed one-off code. The configuration is characterized as modular and scalable, with installation-related setup intended to support adding equipment or stations without changing the core software for each instance. The transcript gives the example that adding a second hospital through a CSV setup can create the associated tags.

The discussion describes hospital locations as having pickup and drop-off relationships. It states that the hospital station pickup ID and hospital station drop-off ID correspond to location IDs, while noting that the primary key or ID column was not shown in the referenced table view. The transcript also states that the current implementation uses a one-to-one relationship between a pickup or drop-off ID and a location, although the model may support one-to-many relationships.

The transcript identifies tipper stations as operator stations and states that each station has two tippers. It distinguishes standard stations from GLD stations and compares the tipper model conceptually with the robotics engine model.

The training material identifies tag read and tag write logs as records of all tags read and written by the system. The displayed Sorter Sweeper Database includes tag paths and values associated with system tags.

The training segment identifies Tipper Departure Activity Model records in the Sorter Sweeper Database. Records are created when an AGV is sent away from the tipper, DropOffSorter, or DropOffHospital.

The training material states that each applicable AGV departure record contains the tote, the tag path, and any fault code. The displayed database table includes fields labeled Task Name, ToteId, Fault, and TagPath, along with tag values.
The recorded tote, tag path, and fault code information can be helpful in narrowing down tipper issues. This is a description of the informational value of the logs, not a troubleshooting procedure.

The system listens to Scan Data 2, sort, and sort-confirm messages from UPS. Items are updated as messages are received and removed when they divert to their final destination. The transcript also refers to recirculation as an item remaining on the sorter.

The transcript identifies package unique ID, tracking number, length, width and height information, weight, and package classification as data supplied by Scan Data 2. The lane activity information also includes package UID, tracking number, length, width, height, and cube.

The item cube adjustment model stores the percentage of cube to use based on package classification. The transcript describes classifications such as boxes, flats, and poly bags, while noting uncertainty about some classification codes. The item default dimension model supplies default dimensions when dimensional data is missing. Envelopes may provide only length, requiring assumed dimensional values. The transcript states that the displayed cube is based on a squashed or implanted cube rather than the actual calculated cube.

The transcript explains that the indicator becomes true when dimension data is missing and default values are picked up. It is used to obtain counts of how much dimensional data was missing. Width and height are described as commonly arriving together, while length is usually present but not always. The transcript gives observed examples of missing-dimension percentages, but these examples are site observations rather than fixed system thresholds.

The lane activity view shows the message type, including Scan Data 2 and sort confirmation. It can associate packages with auto-induct sources using package ID information. The transcript references auto-induct identifiers such as Auto Induct 1 and Auto Induct 2, which are defined by UPS. The view also includes sort-confirm information such as zone and lane number, along with package UID, tracking number, length, width, height, and cube. A package may have missing Scan Data 2 and may therefore lack the expected dimensional information.

The training discussion identifies the Research destinations model as the repository for destinations associated with packages that go off the end of the sorter. The transcript does not define the specific destination values or provide further configuration details.

When a chute is closed, an active exchange is created in the active exchange model. When an empty tote replaces it, the exchange is closed and archived to exchange activity. The active model retains a smaller set of current exchanges, while the activity model stores historical exchange information.

When a bag-out closes as requested, open chutes are closed. Totes containing an item are marked for exchange, and an entry is made in active bag out. The bag-out record is archived to bag out activity once the tote has been tipped.

AGV status model data from GEEK is used for operational notifications concerning RMS faults, AGVs waiting for totes, and AGVs called to maintenance. The E-stop model records the E-stop name, GEEK area ID, and whether the E-stop is active. When an E-stop is released, a record is added to E-stop activity. E-stop duration is recorded as a system metric for zone status reporting.

When UPS cycles a sort, it calls the Reset Metrics API. This opens closed chutes and creates a new SortName and SortGuid. Activity is logged with sort identifiers for historical, sort-to-sort metrics. The referenced Sorter Sweeper Database screen displays sort names, current sort values, and SortGuid values.

The system state model keeps track of system status, including whether chutes are to remain closed after a bag-out and whether sort data is being received. Statuses identified in the training include starting up, startup requested, running, shutdown requested, shutdown, zone configuration requested, zone configuration staging, closeout requested, closeout staging, and closeout staged.

The task model tracks tasks sent to the robotics engine. The described task data includes task ID, task name, tote ID, station, and task status. Completed tasks are archived to task activity. The training compares this active-versus-archived structure with other OptiSweep models.

The training describes database jobs configured to run housekeeping every 12 hours. These jobs delete older data, described as being more than approximately three to seven days old for some data sets, to support memory management. The exact retention period varies and is not fully specified in the segment.

The API Walkthrough slide is identified as page 26 of the training video material and appears at approximately 02:32:04.500. The accompanying transcript is primarily break-related discussion and does not explain the API content.

The training material presents an OptiSweep API suite with GET endpoints for data retrieval and POST endpoints for making requests. The displayed API overview includes System, AGVS, and Totes categories.
Apidog is installed on the primary servers. The source does not specify the installation path, server count, access method, or configuration.

The APIs installed or represented in the OptiSweep environment are also used to feed Ignition. The source does not describe the data flow, interface configuration, refresh behavior, or failure handling.

The displayed catalog includes System endpoints such as System State, System Startup, System Shutdown, CloseOut, Purge, ResetMetrics, SystemMetrics, and zone configuration operations. AGVS endpoints include status retrieval, fault-related data retrieval, and command-related operations. Totes endpoints include tote task retrieval, tote initialization, tote exchange, lane exchange, and exchange-settings operations. These names are presented as API entries; the source does not define their parameters, authorization, or usage sequence.
